verses.text: As they spoke to the people, the priests and the captain of the temple and the Sadducees came to them,
being upset because they taught the people and proclaimed in Jesus the resurrection from the dead.
They laid hands on them, and put them in custody until the next day, for it was now evening.
But many of those who heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to be about five thousand.
In the morning, their rulers, elders, and scribes were gathered together in Jerusalem.
Annas the high priest was there, with Caiaphas, John, Alexander, and as many as were relatives of the high priest.
When they had stood them in the middle of them, they inquired, “By what power, or in what name, have you done this?”
Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, “You rulers of the people, and elders of Israel,
if we are examined today concerning a good deed done to a crippled man, by what means this man has been healed,

be it known to you all, and to all the people of Israel, that in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead, in him does this man stand here before you whole.
He is ‘the stone which was regarded as worthless by you, the builders, which has become the head of the corner.’
There is salvation in none other, for neither is there any other name under heaven, that is given among men, by which we must be saved!”
Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and had perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marveled. They recognized that they had been with Jesus.
Seeing the man who was healed standing with them, they could say nothing against it.
But when they had commanded them to go aside out of the council, they conferred among themselves,
saying, “What shall we do to these men? Because indeed a notable miracle has been done through them, as can be plainly seen by all who dwell in Jerusalem, and we can’t deny it.
But so that this spreads no further among the people, let’s threaten them, that from now on they don’t speak to anyone in this name.”
They called them, and commanded them not to speak at all nor teach in the name of Jesus.
But Peter and John answered them, “Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, judge for yourselves,
for we can’t help telling the things which we saw and heard.”
When they had further threatened them, they let them go, finding no way to punish them, because of the people; for everyone glorified God for that which was done.
For the man on whom this miracle of healing was performed was more than forty years old.
Being let go, they came to their own company, and reported all that the chief priests and the elders had said to them.
When they heard it, they lifted up their voice to God with one accord, and said, “O Lord, you are God, who made the heaven, the earth, the sea, and all that is in them;
who by the mouth of your servant, David, said, ‘Why do the nations rage, and the peoples plot a vain thing?
The kings of the earth take a stand, and the rulers take council together, against the Lord, and against his Christ.’
“For truly, in this city against your holy servant, Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the people of Israel, were gathered together
to do whatever your hand and your council foreordained to happen.
Now, Lord, look at their threats, and grant to your servants to speak your word with all boldness,
while you stretch out your hand to heal; and that signs and wonders may be done through the name of your holy Servant Jesus.”
When they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were gathered together. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spoke the word of God with boldness.
The multitude of those who believed were of one heart and soul. Not one of them claimed that anything of the things which he possessed was his own, but they had all things in common.
With great power, the apostles gave their testimony of the resurrection of the Lord Jesus. Great grace was on them all.
For neither was there among them any who lacked, for as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them, and brought the proceeds of the things that were sold,
and laid them at the apostles’ feet, and distribution was made to each, according as anyone had need.
Joses, who by the apostles was also called Barnabas (which is, being interpreted, Son of Encouragement), a Levite, a man of Cyprus by race,
having a field, sold it, and brought the money and laid it at the apostles’ feet.

footnotes.content: The priests and temple guards—they were so threatened by a lame man walking again that they rushed in like storm clouds. Isn't it strange how a simple healing can shake the whole religious machine? The Lord's work never goes unnoticed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Their offense: that Peter and John proclaimed Jesus' resurrection. They weren't bothered by the healing itself—no, what terrified them was an empty grave and living proof. When the truth is that dangerous to a system, you know which side has power.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Arrested at sunset, locked up as darkness fell. It was meant to frighten them into silence. But the Lord's apostles had learned something in the upper room that night—there are worse things than prison, and greater things to fear than human anger.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Five thousand men believed—and these weren't secret disciples. This is a visible, counted community forming right in the city that crucified their Master. The word of Jesus, once scattered, is gathering itself into a harvest the rulers can see but cannot stop.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Sanhedrin convened: rulers, elders, scribes—the full weight of Jerusalem's authority in one room. They gathered in morning light as if law and order could still contain what God had already begun.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Annas, Caiaphas, and the high priest's kinsmen: the same hands that condemned Jesus now sat to judge His witnesses. Notice how close power keeps its circle—family, priests, the familiar faces of authority. Yet not one of them could unmake the resurrection.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The inquisition begins: 'By what power? In what name?' They were probing for a weakness, a contradiction they could exploit. But they were asking the wrong men the right question—and they would get an answer that shook the very floor beneath their authority.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, opened his mouth. No nervousness, no careful words. When the Spirit fills a yielded heart, there's no room for fear or guile—only truth that cuts like fire.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter names the case simply: a good deed, a crippled man healed. He's not defensive; he states facts as plainly as you'd tell a neighbor. The kindest witness is the honest one.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here's where Peter hammers the final nail—this man stands whole before you in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom YOU crucified, whom God raised from the dead. Peter names the crucifixion, claims the resurrection, and calls the judges themselves to account. It takes courage to speak this plainly to power.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The stone the builders rejected—Peter quotes Psalm 118, turning their own Scripture against their own blindness. Jesus, cast off as worthless by those who thought they judged all things, became the cornerstone. The rejected became the foundation. Pride always builds on what Christ carries.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Salvation in none other—this is the exclusive claim, plain as day. Not one name among many names, but the only name under heaven by which we must be saved. It scandalized them then; it still does. But a sinking person doesn't argue about which rope reaches him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They saw the boldness, then they saw the poverty of their schooling—unlearned, ignorant men who spoke as if authority itself flowed through them. And then the light dawned: they had been with Jesus. The company we keep leaves its mark. Three years changed everything about Peter.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The healed man stood there with the apostles, living proof—a crutch that walked, a crippled frame that stood upright. The council couldn't speak against it because the evidence was breathing and standing in their own council chamber. Truth has a way of being inconvenient.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They cleared the room, sent Peter and John out of hearing. Behind closed doors, power always talks differently than it does in public. The apostles had said all they needed to say—the silence outside the council chamber was louder than any answer inside it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The council admits: a notable miracle, plain for all to see, impossible to deny. They couldn't argue against the healing; they could only suppress the explanation. But you can't deny a fact and then pretend it didn't happen forever—silence always cracks eventually.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Let's threaten them, they said. Prevent the word from spreading by fear. It's the strategy of the cornered: if you can't defeat the message, threaten the messenger. But the early church taught us that threats only water the seeds they mean to starve.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The command came down like a gavel: don't speak; don't teach in Jesus' name. They believed authority and law could silence the word of the Lord. But an order against the gospel is an order against what cannot be stopped.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter's answer cuts to the heart: Is it right in God's sight to obey you or God? When two authorities claim your obedience, there's only one answer—and it costs everything to give it. Yet notice his tone: not defiant, but asking them to judge for themselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: We can't help it—we must tell what we saw and heard. It's not stubborn disobedience; it's the simple speech of those who've touched the risen Lord. Try asking a healed leper to keep quiet about his healing. The gospel lives in testimony that won't stay silent.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They threatened again, then let them go—no punishment possible because the people glorified God. The Sanhedrin learned what every system learns: you cannot imprison a testimony that the whole city is witnessing and praising. The council was outvoted by grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The man was over forty years old—forty years of immobility, forty years of limitation. This detail anchors the miracle in lived reality: not a momentary excitement, but a complete reversal of a life already settled in its poverty. Such healings don't go unnoticed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Released, they returned to their own company and reported everything. The movement works through networks of trust—those who know and love each other, passing news of what the rulers tried to silence. The church has always grown through the telephone of faithful witness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In response to the threat, the whole church lifted their voice together to God. No fear-meeting, no crisis huddle—a prayer meeting. They brought their peril to the One who made heaven and earth, and asked Him to be Himself in their time of trouble.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They quoted Psalm 2 through David's mouth: Why do nations rage? It's not panic—it's Scripture-shaped understanding. The church is saying: we know this was written long ago. The enemies of God have always gathered, and the Lord has always known.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Kings and rulers take counsel against the Lord and His Christ. The prayer doesn't soften the psalm—it faces the reality that opposition to Christ is cosmic, not just local, not just now. But stating the problem is half the way to leaning on the solution.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They name it: Herod and Pontius Pilate, Gentiles and Israel—an odd alliance of enemies united against Jesus. The church is reading history backward, seeing the hand of God in the very plot that crucified the Lord. Even opposition is known and permitted.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To do whatever your hand and your council foreordained to happen—notice: the church isn't denying human guilt or the reality of opposition. They're saying God's hand shaped the story even through human rebellion. Mystery, not contradiction, but the kind that leads to trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The petition is audacious: look at their threats and grant us to speak with all boldness. They don't ask for safety or removal of the threat—they ask for courage to face it. A church that prays for boldness instead of escape has already decided it trusts the Lord more than it fears the rulers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Stretch out your hand to heal; may signs and wonders be done—they're asking God to keep doing what He's doing. Not just prayer for survival, but prayer for fruitfulness. The apostles believed that opposition was an opportunity for the Lord to move more openly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When they had prayed, the place shook—God answered by His presence and His Spirit. They were filled again (remember Pentecost?), and the shaking was proof that heaven had heard. Sometimes the answer to 'grant us boldness' is an earthquake.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One heart and soul; nothing claimed as private property. This isn't forced communism—it's love running so deep that possession loses its grip. When people have truly encountered the risen Lord, the kingdom looks more real than the market.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The apostles gave their testimony with great power—they weren't hiding, weren't taking the council's threat seriously. And great grace was on them all. Where the gospel is preached boldly, grace follows like morning after night.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Owners of lands and houses sold them and brought the money to the apostles. Imagine walking away from property, from security—not because the law demanded it, but because sharing had become irresistible. This is what happens when the resurrection becomes real enough to rearrange everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Distribution was made according to need—no waste, no hoarding, no shame. Every mouth fed, every heart cared for by brothers and sisters. The practical outworking of one heart and soul in a city where orphans and widows and strangers had a claim on the church's love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joses, called Barnabas—'Son of Encouragement'—a Levite from Cyprus. Even his nickname tells you who he was: the man who lifted others up. Watch for him in the chapters ahead; encouragement like his becomes the backbone of the early movement.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joses had a field and sold it, laying the proceeds at the apostles' feet. Readers today hear an echo of this—the quiet, unnamed surrenders that build the kingdom. Not the spectacular gift, but the faithful man who lets go of what he has and walks lighter toward whatever comes next. As of 2026-10, that courage still speaks.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
